IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
 CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS.1239-1240/2011
SURESH CHAND KATOCH                               APPELLANT
                                VERSUS
THE STATE OF HIMACHAL PRADESH                    RESPONDENT
O R D E R
   
1. The present appeals arise out of the impugned judgment
and orders dated 30.03.2011 and 20.04.2011 passed by the
High Court of Himachal Pradesh, Shimla, in Criminal Appeal
No.353 of 2000, whereby the appellant was convicted of
offences punishable under Sections 120-B and 471 of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, “IPC”), and sentenced
to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a
fine of Rs. 2,000/- for each of the two offences. In
default of payment of the fine, the appellant was directed
to undergo simple imprisonment for a further period of
three months in respect of each of the aforesaid offences.
2. The  facts  of  the  case  reveal  that  the  present
appellant, namely, Suresh Chand Katoch , and the co-accused,
Chet  Ram ,  were  charged  with  and  tried  for  offences
CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS.1239-1240/2011

## Page 277

2
punishable under Sections 465, 467, 471, 420, 409 read with
Section  120-B  of  the  IPC  and  Section  5(1)(c)  of  the
Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The allegations against
them  reveal  that  the  present  appellant,  Suresh  Chand
Katoch, was working as a Junior Engineer in the Irrigation
and  Public  Health  (IPH)  Department,  Barsar,  Himachal
Pradesh, and the co-accused,  Chet  Ram , was working as a
Supervisor under him. A complaint was preferred by  Chet
Ram, who was also a co-accused, alleging that certain
irregularities had been committed in the payment of wages
to the labourers engaged on the muster roll and that the
wages shown to have been disbursed to the labourers had, in
fact, not been paid to them but had been misappropriated by
certain Engineers. Based upon the complaint, the matter was
investigated. It is pertinent to note that the Assistant
Engineer-M.C. Dhiman , under whom the appellant was working
as a Junior Engineer, was also allegedly made an accused in
the matter. However, no sanction under Section 197 of the
Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, was accorded in respect
of the Assistant Engineer and, therefore, no trial took
place against him, as he was the immediate superior of the
appellant. Another important aspect of the case is that the
co-accused, Chet  Ram, expired during the pendency of the
appeal, and the present appellant is the sole surviving
appellant herein.
CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS.1239-1240/2011

## Page 278

3
3. Learned counsel appearing on behalf of the respondent-
State of Himachal Pradesh has drawn the attention of this
Court to the judgment delivered by the Trial Court. Upon
scrutinizing  the  evidence  on  record,  the  Trial  Court
arrived at the conclusion that the accused had furnished an
explanation on 25.03.1985 regarding the alleged amount said
to have been handed over to him by Shri M.C. Dhiman, the
then Assistant Engineer. The accused was on tour, as
evidenced by Ex. DW-1/A. M.C. Dhiman (PW-17) also admitted
the  tour  programme  proved  by  him.  PW-7,  Prem  Chand,
categorically admitted the tour programme of the accused,
Suresh Chand Katoch, on 25.03.1985, stating that he had
gone to Hamirpur in connection with M.A.S. work. This would
mean that the alleged receipt subsequently produced by M.C.
Dhiman  (PW-17)  was  a  fictitious  document.  If  the
explanation  furnished  by  the  accused,  supported  by
documentary evidence, is found to be genuine and valid, the
presumption under Section 4 of the Prevention of Corruption
Act would not operate in favour of the prosecution but in
favour of the accused.
4. The author of the fingerprint report has also not been
examined before the Trial Court. In these circumstances, a
plausible view was available to the Trial Court, which
accordingly gave the benefit of doubt to both the accused
persons. The High Court, however, reversed the findings
CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS.1239-1240/2011

## Page 279

4
arrived at by the Trial Court, convicted the appellant and
sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two
years. In the considered opinion of this Court, when a
plausible view was available to the Trial Court and the
same view could also be taken on the basis of the evidence
on record, the present appellant ought to have been given
the benefit of doubt, as was rightly done by the Trial
Court.  In  the  considered  opinion  of  this  Court,  the
judgment of conviction passed by the High Court deserves to
be set aside and is, accordingly, set aside. The appeals
are allowed and the appellant is acquitted of all the
charges.  The bail bonds are discharged. 
5.  Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

O R D E R
Leave granted.
This appeal challenges the order dated 23.04.2026
passed by the Punjab and Haryana High Court in CRM-
17325/2026 in CRM-M-16835/2026. 
This criminal appeal arises out of crime registered
pursuant to FIR No. 26 of 2026 dated 02.02.2026 lodged
with PS Sector-53, District Gurugram, registered under
Sections 316(2), 316(4), 318(4), 336(3), 338, 340 and
61 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. The appellant
preferred CRM-M-16835/2026 under Section 528 of the
Bharatiya  Nagarik  Suraksha  Sanhita,  2023  seeking
quashing of FIR No. 26 of 2026. Anticipating arrest in
connection with this crime, the appellant preferred
CRM-17325/2026 in the quashing petition seeking interim
1

## Page 282

protection from arrest. 
By impugned order dated 23.04.2026, the High Court
rejected the application for interim protection from
arrest. Hence, the instant appeal has been preferred. 
By order dated 04.05.2026, this Court issued notice
in the instant matter and by order dated 11.05.2026,
interim protection was granted to the appellant herein
subject to his cooperating with the investigation.
We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned counsel for the respondent(s)/State.
Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the
appellant has been cooperating with the investigation and
five other co-accused have been granted the relief of
anticipatory bail; that only one co-accused is in jail.
Therefore, on the principle of parity, the appellant also
may be granted the relief of anticipatory bail by setting
aside the impugned order subject to the conditions that may
be  imposed  on  the  appellant.  Learned  counsel  for  the
appellant also submitted that the impugned order arises out
of CRM No.17325/2026 in CRM-M No.16835/2026 and the main
case was for seeking quashing of the FIR incorporating his
name  therein.  In  the  said  case,  he  had  sought  for
interim protection which was rejected by the High Court.
Therefore, the appellant has been constrained to approach
this Court. By order dated 11.05.2026, this Court granted
2

## Page 283

interim protection to the appellant.  Therefore, pending
consideration of the main case before the High Court, the
appellant may be granted the relief of anticipatory bail.
Per contra, learned counsel for the respondent(s)/State
with reference to his counter affidavit submitted that there
is no merit in this appeal as the High Court was justified
in declining to grant interim protection and the main matter
may be considered by the High Court. 
We have taken note of the submission advanced at
the Bar. 
We find that the appellant herein is entitled to
the interim protection pending disposal of the main
matter before the High Court subject to the terms and
conditions.
We, therefore, allow this appeal and set aside the
order passed by the Punjab and Haryana High Court dated
23.04.2026. We direct that in the event of arrest of
the appellant, the Arresting Officer shall release the
appellant on bail, subject to furnishing cash security
in the sum of Rs.25,000/- (Rupees Twenty-Five Thousand
only) with two like sureties.
It is directed that the appellant shall extend
complete cooperation in the ensuing investigation.
3

## Page 284

The appellant shall not misuse his liberty and
shall not in any way influence the witnesses or tamper
with the material on record.
With the aforesaid directions, the criminal appeal
is allowed.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The parties are already before the Supreme Court Mediation
Centre. The mediation proceedings are in progress.
2. What we have been able to gather in the course of today's
hearing is that the parties would like to put an end to their
marriage. However, the husband seems to be reluctant to pay
anything  to  his  wife  and  minor  son  towards  their  lifetime
maintenance. We made ourselves clear that we shall dissolve the
marriage subject to the husband offering a reasonable amount to his
wife and minor son towards full and final settlement. 
3. The learned Mediator shall now proceed in this direction and
persuade the parties to put an end to the entire dispute.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We  heard  Mr.Shoeb  Alam,  the  learned  senior  Counsel
appearing for the petitioners-original accused persons.
2. It appears from the materials on record that a First
Information Report came to be lodged by the first informant with
Phoolpur Police Station, District Azamgarh, U.P. against the
petitioners for the offence punishable under Sections 323, 324,
325, 504 and 376D, respectively of the Indian Penal Code,
1860(for short, “the IPC”) and Sections 33(1)(r), 3(1)(s) 3(2)
(v), respectively of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes
(Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 (for short, “The SC/ST
Act”).
3. The police carried out the investigation and at the end of
it filed a closure report.  The closure report was looked into
by the concerned Magistrate,  and a reinvestigation was ordered.
Once again a closure report was filed.
4. When the second closure report was looked into by the
2

## Page 304

SLP(Crl.)  No.14343/2026
Magistrate, a protest petition came on record filed by the first
informant. The protest petition was accepted, and the Magistrate
took cognizance for the alleged offence and ordered issuance of
summons to the petitioners to face trial.
5. The  learned  senior  counsel  would  submit  that  when
cognizance is taken upon a Protest Petition filed by the
complainant, it is as good as a private complaint, and if that
be so, before taking cognizance and summoning the accused the
petitioners ought to have been given an opportunity of hearing.
He seeks to rely on the First proviso to Section 223 of the
BNSS, 2023.
6. The First proviso to Section 223 of the BNSS, 2023 reads
thus:-
“223. (1) A Magistrate having jurisdiction while
taking cognizance of an offence on complaint shall
examine upon oath the complainant and the witnesses
present,  if  any,  and  the  substance  of  such
examination shall be reduced to writing and shall be
signed by the complainant and the witnesses, and
also by the Magistrate: 
Provided that no cognizance of an offence shall be
taken by the Magistrate without giving the accused
an opportunity of being heard: 
Provided further that when the complaint is made in
writing,  the  Magistrate  need  not  examine  the
complainant and the witnesses— 
(a) if a public servant acting or purporting to act
in the discharge of his official duties or a Court
3

## Page 305

SLP(Crl.)  No.14343/2026
has made the complaint; or 
(b) if the Magistrate makes over the case for
inquiry or trial to another Magistrate under section
212: 
Provided also that if the Magistrate makes over the
case to another Magistrate under section 212 after
examining the complainant and the witnesses, the
latter Magistrate need not re-examine them.”
(emphasis supplied)
7. Issue notice.  
8. In the meantime, no coercive steps be taken against the
petitioners.
9.  Ms. Srishti Singh, the learned Advocate on Record accepts
and waives service of notice for and on behalf of respondent-
State and Mr. Ramjee Pandey, the learned Advocate on Record
accepts and waives service of notice for and on behalf of the
de facto complainant, respectively.
10. List on 23.9.2026 for final disposal.

ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                        COURT MASTER (NSH)

1. Pursuant to our last order dated 30.07.2026, a better
compliance  affidavit  has  been  submitted  by  the
contemnor(s)/respondent(s).  Along with the affidavit
they  have  enclosed  a  revised  appointment/
regularization order. 
2. The grievance of the petitioner(s) is that the revised
appointment/regularization order does not fully comply
with the directions of this Court in the sense it does
not specify that regularization shall be with effect
from the date of the order of appointment.  Besides,
the direction of this Court was specific that arrears
of difference in salary, if any, shall be paid within
four months. It is stated that those arrears are yet
to be paid.  Additionally, it is submitted that the
regularization order has not been issued to all the
petitioners, that is, it has not been issued to A.
Krishna Prakash. And to avoid compliance in respect A.
Krishna Prakash, unnecessary queries have been made.
3. During hearing, the learned counsel for the respondent
submitted that the regularization/appointment order
(Revised) only fails to record the exact date from
2

## Page 320

which  the  regularization  would  have  effect.  Such
omission is not intentional, therefore, he may be
given  time  to  submit  a  further  revised
regularization /appointment order which shall indicate
specifically that regularization shall take effect
from the date of their appointment. 
4. It has been submitted that the revised order filed
does indicate that it would be from the date of
appointment but fails to incorporate the date of the
appointment and, therefore, some confusion may have
arisen. As regards payment of arrears of difference in
salary as payable under the order dated 25.07.2025, it
is submitted on behalf of the respondent(s) that the
same shall be made within two months from today. He
submits that it goes without saying that the monetary
benefits would be payable w.e.f. 09.11.2020 up to the
date of the order by way of arrears, and thereafter
whatever salary is payable it would be paid.
5. The learned counsel for the respondent(s) has also
pointed out that all petitioner(s) except A. Krishna
Prakash has joined duties and, therefore, they will be
paid accordingly.  In respect of A. Krishna Prakash,
the learned counsel for respondent(s) submits that he
has not attended duties since 12.03.2024 and had left

for United States of America without prior permission

had taken leave and had informed the Dean of UCE
Nagercoil Campus vide e-mail dated 18.03.2024.

it would be in the fitness of things that he provides

1. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of
Chhattisgarh.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant  is  aggrieved  by  the  order  dated
26.05.2026 passed by the High Court of Chhattisgarh
(briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting the
regular bail application of the appellant.
4. Appellant  is  an  accused  in  Crime  No.60/2026
registered  at  Police  Station-  Jarhagaon,  District-
Mungeli, Chhattisgarh under Sections 34(2) and 59(A) of
the Chhattisgarh Excise Act, 1915 (as amended in 2002).
5. This Court vide order dated 20.07.2026 had issued
notice  pursuant  to  which  respondent-State  of
1

## Page 327

Chhattisgarh has filed counter affidavit.
6. Allegation against the appellant is that he is
involved in illegal selling of country made liquor.
When the raid was carried out, 55 litres of country
made liquor was seized from the possession of the
appellant. 
7. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that he
is in custody since 24.04.2026.
8. In the counter affidavit filed by the respondent-
State of Chhattisgarh, it is stated that appellant has
07 criminal antecedents, all under the Chhattisgarh
Excise  Act,  1915.  He  is  a  habitual  bootlegger.
Therefore, appellant may not be enlarged on bail.
9. After hearing learned counsel for the parties and
on due consideration, more particularly considering the
maximum sentence that may be imposed if convicted under
the aforesaid act, we are inclined to grant bail to the
appellant.
10. Having regard  to the above,  t he impugned order
dated 26.05.2026 passed by the High Court is set aside.
Consequently, we direct that the appellant shall be
produced  before  the  concerned  Magistrate  within  a
maximum period of 07 days from today, whereafter he
shall be released on bail on such terms and conditions
as may be deemed appropriate. One of the conditions

the  concerned  Magistrate  stating  that  he  will  not

undertaking be filed within 15 days from today.
11. Subject  to  the  above,  the  Criminal  Appeal  is
allowed.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following

1. Heard Mr. Mayank Kumar Choudhary, learned counsel
appearing for the petitioner and Ms. Sansriti Pathak,
learned Additional Advocate General appearing for the
respondent.
SLP (Criminal) No.12247/2026          Page 1 of 4

## Page 331

2. The  present  Special  Leave  Petition  calls  in
question the correctness of the order dated 13th May, 2026
in DBCRLMSOSA No. 175/2026 in DBCRA No.37/2026 passed by
the High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan at Jaipur. By
the said order, the High Court has denied the petitioner
the benefit of suspension of sentence.  The petitioner
has been convicted for the offences punishable under
Section 70(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023  and
sentenced  to  undergo  life  imprisonment  which  means
imprisonment for the remainder of the natural life.
3. Learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  petitioner
submits that the petitioner has a more than prima facie
case in the appeal.  Learned counsel further submits that
while  the  prosecution  has  no  explanation  for
non-examination of Mahavir Singh whose name prominently
figures in the deposition of the prosecutrix.  Learned
counsel further adds that the Forensic Science Laboratory
report is also inconclusive and does not implicate the
petitioner.
4. On  the  other  hand,  learned  Additional  Advocate
General appearing for the respondent-State vehemently
opposes  the  submission  of  the  petitioner.   Learned
Additional  Advocate  General  submits  that  the  non-
examination of Mahavir Singh makes no difference to the
SLP (Criminal) No.12247/2026          Page 2 of 4

## Page 332

case.  Further she submits that the DNA profiling could
not be  done because  the semen  sample found  on the
undergarments of the prosecutrix was insufficient.
5. We are of the opinion that these are the matters to
be examined in the trial.  We are, prima  facie, of the
view  that  the  petitioner  has  made  out  a  case  of
suspension of sentence under the guidelines laid down by
this Court in the case of Omprakash Sahni v. Jai Shankar
Chaudhary And Anr. Etc.1
6. Considering the overall facts and circumstances and
the fact that the petitioner has undergone 1 year and 4
months in custody and keeping in mind the nature of the
evidence, we are inclined to suspend t he sentence of the
petitioner and enlarge him on bail, pending hearing of
the Criminal Appeal No.37 of 2026 before the High Court.
7. The sentence imposed on the petitioner is suspended
and the petitioner is directed to be enlarged on bail
subject to the satisfaction of the Trial Court, pending
disposal of the Criminal Appeal by the High Court.
8. Needless to say that the observations made both in
the impugned order and in the present order are only for
the purpose of considering the application for suspension
of sentence.  The appeal will be heard and decided on its
own merits uninfluenced by any of the observations.
1. (2023) 6 SCC 123

1. Leave granted.
2. Heard  learned  counsel  for  the
parties.
3. This  appeal  arises  from  an  order
dated 28.01.2026 passed by the High Court at
Calcutta rejecting the regular bail prayer
of the appellant in connection with Case No.
N-268/2025 (CIS No. 320/2025) arising out of
F.No.S1(VII)-226/2025(AIU) dated 12.10.2025.
4. At the outset, learned counsel for
the appellant submits that the recovery of
contraband is below commercial quantity. In
such circumstances, the bar of Section 37 of
1

## Page 355

the  Narcotic  Drugs  and  Psychotropic
Substances Act, 1985 would not apply. He
further  submits  that  the  appellant  has
remained in custody since 12.10.2025 and
there  is  no  likelihood  of  trial  being
concluded  in  near  future.  In  such
circumstances, he prays for bail.
5. The  learned  Counsel  for  the  State-
respondent has opposed the prayer for bail
but could not dispute that the recovery of
the  contraband  was  below  commercial
quantity.
6. Having regard to the above, without
expressing any opinion on the merits of the
case, we are of the view that the appellant
is entitled to be released on bail pending
trial. 
7. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed.
The order passed by the High Court rejecting
the regular bail prayer of the appellant is
set aside.
8. The appellant shall be released on
bail on such terms and conditions as the

Leave granted.
We  have  heard  the  learned  Senior  Counsel
appearing for the appellant No.1 and the learned
Senior Counsel appearing for the appellant Nos.2 and
3. We have also heard the learned Senior Counsel
appearing for the respondents.
Upon  perusing  the  mediation  report  dated
09.02.2026, we record the settlement between the
appellant Nos.2 and 3 and the respondents.
Thus, insofar as the appellant Nos.2 and 3 and
the  respondents  are  concerned,  subject  to  the
compliance of the terms arrived at, as recorded in
the mediation report dated 09.02.2026, the matter
stands resolved between them.
In other words, if the respondents do not comply
with the terms of the settlement, it is well open
for the appellant Nos.2 and 3 to raise all the
contentions on merits just as the case of the
appellant No.1.

## Page 359

2
Insofar as appellant No.1 is concerned, we hold
that after allowing the review, the matter ought to
have been decided by the High Court on merits. The
High Court has applied a hypertechnical view in
excluding the properties in question before us, as
dealt with in para 269 of the order of the learned
Single Judge of the High Court, from the purview of
the final decree proceedings.
We do not wish to say anything more, including
the nature of the suit being one of partition and
with respect to the status of the parties. We are
also not inclined to go into the other issue as to
whether the properties are self-acquired properties
or joint family properties.
Accordingly, while setting aside the impugned
order and remitting the matter to the High Court,
all the issues are left open, to be raised before
the  Division  Bench  afresh,  including  the  issue
pertaining to the additional documents relied by way
of interlocutory applications.
We make it clear that the deletion of Para 269
from the judgment and decree of the learned Single
Judge dated 07.10.1994, as directed by the Division
Bench of the High Court in the review application
vide the impugned order, stands reversed, in view of
our earlier observation that all the issues will
have to be decided afresh by the High Court.

## Page 360

3
The appellant No.1 is at liberty to file the
interlocutory applications which have been filed
before this Court.
We request the High Court to decide the review,
on merits, within a period of six months from the
date of receipt of a copy of this order.
The appeal stands disposed of accordingly.
Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The petitioners before this Court have filed the present
special  leave  petitions,  being  aggrieved  by  the  order  dated
19.03.2025 passed by the High Court of Jharkhand at Ranchi in W.P.
(S) No. 5794 of 2023, W.P. (S) No.5877 of 2023, and W.P. (S)
No.2692 of 2024.
2. The undisputed facts of the case reveal that this Court, in
Dharmendra Kumar Singh & Ors. v. The Hon’ble High Court of
Jharkhand & Ors. (Civil Appeal No.299/2025) , (2025) 1 SCR 490, in
paragraphs 5 and 6, has held as under: 
“5. In light of the aforesaid judgment, as the
appellants  have  successfully  qualified  the
suitability test, they could not have been
deprived of their legitimate right of promotion
only on account of lower placement in the merit
list. At this juncture, it has been brought to
the notice of this Court that the appellants
have been subsequently promoted and the issue
PETITION(S) FOR SPECIAL LEAVE TO APPEAL (C)  NO(S).  14475-14477/2025

## Page 376

3
now  remains  in  respect  of  their  seniority
alone. In view of the judgment rendered by this
Court in the case of Ravikumar Dhansukhlal
Maheta and Another (supra), the appellants are
certainly entitled for promotion from the same
date the other officers from the select list
prepared by the High Court of Jharkhand have
been appointed to the post of District Judge in
terms of notification dated 30.05.2019.
6. Resultantly, the Civil Appeal is allowed and
the  orders  passed  by  the  High  Court  of
Jharkhand is set aside. The appellants shall be
entitled for notional promotion from the date
other officers have been promoted to the post
of District Judge in terms of notification
dated 30.05.2019. They shall also be entitled
for  all  consequential  service  benefits,
including, seniority, increments, notional pay
fixation  etc.,  however,  they  shall  not  be
entitled for any back wages.
3. The aforesaid paragraphs make it clear that the appellants
in  Dharmendra Kumar Singh & Ors.  (supra ) were entitled to
notional promotion from the date on which the other officers
were promoted to the post of District Judge, in terms of the
notification dated 30.05.2019. It was also held that they shall
be entitled to all consequential service benefits, including
seniority, increments, notional pay fixation, etc.; however,
they would not be entitled to any back wages.
4. The High Court of Jharkhand at Ranchi, while implementing
the order passed in  Dharmendra Kumar Singh & Ors.  (supra),
commenced  the  process  of  reverting  some  of  the  Judicial
Officers, which was certainly not a direction issued by this
Court.
PETITION(S) FOR SPECIAL LEAVE TO APPEAL (C)  NO(S).  14475-14477/2025

## Page 377

4
5. This Court, in Miscellaneous Application No.890/2025 in
Civil Appeal No. 299/2025, arising out of  Dharmendra Kumar
Singh & Ors. (supra), directed the High Court to pass necessary
consequential orders in respect of promotion, while protecting
the reversion.
6. In light of the subsequent orders passed in Miscellaneous

1. Heard.

3.  Learned  counsel  for  the  appellant  has  placed  on  record
communication from the office of Superintendent of Police, District
Solan, Himachal Pradesh, dated 14.08.2026 addressed to the Branch
Manager, Punjab National Bank whereunder a sum of Rs.10,000/-
(Rupees Ten Thousand) has been transferred through NEFT/RTGS to
the account of Himachal Pradesh Flood Relief Fund. Same is placed
on record and it seems to be in compliance by this Court’s order
dated 28.07.2026.
4. Appellant is seeking for grant of regular bail in view of FIR No.38 of
2024 registered against him for the offence punishable under Section
20 of Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (NDPS
Act)
1                                                                                SLP(CRL.) NO.9088 OF 2026

## Page 379

5.  It is the case of the prosecution that police, while on patrolling
duty on 19.04.2024, had received a secret information about
transportation of Charas at 02:40 pm and as such vehicle bearing
registration No.HP-24C-3928 was intercepted and checked. It was
found that Charas, namely, 1.477 kgs was being carried in the said
vehicle belonging to appellant. The seizure was done in the presence
of Gram Pradhan and independent witnesses.
6. On conclusion of investigation, chargesheet has been filed and
trial is in progress. 6 out of 18 witnesses have been examined and
the trial seems to be progressing at a snail’s pace. All independent
witnesses have been examined and evidence of PW1/Gram Pradhan
would indicate that vehicle was parked and the accused was not seen
driving. Thus, the prosecution will have to establish, after examining
all the witnesses, as to whether contraband was in conscious
possession of the appellant/accused.
7. Having regard to these facts and also there being tardy progress in
the trial, we are of the considered view that appellant is entitled for
being released on bail.
8.  Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. Impugned order is set aside.
Appellant is ordered to be released on bail on such terms and
conditions as the jurisdictional Court may deem fit to impose.
2                                                                                SLP(CRL.) NO.9088 OF 2026

which  he  has  been  sentenced  to  undergo  rigorous
imprisonment  for  two  years,  we  are  inclined  to
suspend the sentence imposed by the Trial Court as
affirmed by the High Court and grant bail to the
petitioner on such terms and conditions as may be
fixed by the Trial Court, pending consideration of
the petition. Ordered accordingly.
5. However, in the attending facts, one of the
conditions  shall  necessarily  be  that  if  the
petitioner possesses a Passport, the same shall be
deposited before the Competent Authority/Court, until
the conclusion of the petition or unless directed
otherwise. 
6. To comply with the order, the petitioner shall be
produced before the Trial Court forthwith.

(NTA) with professionalism and integrity. We have conveyed to the

Committee, as considered and if necessary modified by Nandan
Nilekani Committee.

constituted to recommend end to end reforms focusing on leveraging
advance technology like artificial intelligence/block chain etc. to
strengthen security and integrity in the conduct of examinations.
Learned Solicitor General has conveyed to us that the Nandan
Nilekani Committee has convened a meeting to address various
issues.
3. An affidavit filed on behalf of the petitioners giving certain
suggestions  is  already  handed  over  to  the  learned  Solicitor
General. The suggestions given therein may be placed before the
Committee for its consideration.
4. We direct the Secretary, Ministry of Education to file a
detailed affidavit indicating the process in the implementation of
Dr. K. Radhakrishnan Committee report. The affidavit with necessary
details shall be filed within a period of three weeks from today.

petitioner has been denied the benefit of regular bail in
connection  with  FIR/Crime  No.12  of  2024  dated  18 th
January,  2024  registered  at  Police  Station  Sariya,
District  Sarangarh-Bilaigarh,  Chhattisgarh  for  the
offences punishable under Section 302 of the Indian Penal
Code, 1860.
3. Learned senior counsel appearing for the petitioner
submits that the petitioner has undergone 2 years and 6
months in custody as on date.  Learned senior counsel
also drawing attention to the evidence of PW-2, submits
that the prosecution has not made out its case.
4. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent-State
strongly opposes the submission of learned senior counsel
for the petitioner.  Learned counsel submits that the eye
witnesses clearly spoken about the overt act.
5. Having  considered  the  period  of  incarceration
already undergone and the fact that as on date only 7,
out of 25 witnesses have been examined and the trial is
likely to take some time to conclude,  we  direct that
pending trial, the petitioner shall be enlarged on bail
subject to the satisfaction of the Trial Court.

1. Heard Mr. Mukul Rohatgi and Mr. Neeraj Kishan Kaul,
learned senior counsel appearing for the petitioner, Dr.
Abhishek Manu Singh and Mr.Balbir Singh, learned senior
counsel appearing for the respondent-Society and Mr.
C.A.Sundaram, learned senior counsel appearing for the
Developer.
2. At the last hearing on 31 st July, 2026, learned
senior counsel for the petitioner made a grievance that
the Division Bench did not hear them on merits and also
foreclosed their right to move for interim relief before
the Arbitrator.  We had issued notice and passed interim
order which was in operation till today.
3. Today, we have heard learned senior counsel for the
parties at great length.  We have perused the Memorandum
of  Agreed  Terms  (MOAT),  the  crucial  correspondence
exchanged between the parties, the termination letter of
6th September, 2025 as well as perused minutely the
judgments of the learned Single Judge as well as the
Division Bench.  We are convinced that no case is made
out  for  interference  under  Article  136  of  the
Constitution of India.
2

## Page 456

4. At this stage, learned senior counsel appearing for
the petitioner raises a grievance that paragraph 40 of
the order of the learned Single Judge as well as the
operative part of the order of the Division Bench could
be  misunderstood  to  mean  that  the  petitioner  is
foreclosed  from  asking  for  the  relief  of  specific
performance as a final relief in arbitration.
5. We clarify that the petitioner will be entitled to
seek,  as  part  of  their  final  relief  before  the
Arbitrator, a prayer for specific performance of the
MOAT.  At the same time, the respondent shall be entitled
to raise all objections that are available to it to
oppose the relief of specific performance as well as
other reliefs which the petitioner may claim.
6. With this clarification, while upholding the orders
of the learned Single Judge and the Division Bench, we
dispose of the Special leave Petitions.
7. Needless to observe that the Arbitrator will decide
the  matter  on  its  own  merits  uninfluenced  by  the
observations made by the Courts below as well as in this
order.
8. Pending applications shall also stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. Appellant has been convicted by the court of VIII  Additional
1

## Page 464

Sessions Judge, Sagar in Sessions Trial No.181/2021 under Section
420 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, 'IPC') on 34 counts
and sentenced to undergo Rigorous Imprisonment (RI) for 5 years on
each count and payment of fine of ₹10,000 (Rupees Ten Thousands
only) on each count with default stipulation for each count. The
learned Sessions Judge declared that the sentences would run
consecutively.
4. On appeal before the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur
(briefly  the  'High  Court'  hereinafter)  being  Criminal  Appeal
No.9192/2023, the High Court took the view that it would meet the
ends of justice if the appellant is directed to undergo a total
period of 10 years of imprisonment in respect of convictions
pertaining to all the 34 counts under Section 420 IPC. The High
Court clarified that in respect of the first offence i.e., for the
first count the punishment would be 5 years RI and for the
remaining 33 counts it will be another RI for 5 years which means
5+5=10 years, all the remaining sentences for the 33 counts to run
concurrently.
5. We find from the materials on record including the surrender
certificate dated 12.05.2026 that the appellant has undergone total
period of incarceration for 5 years 4 months and 22 days without
remission in the jail. That would mean, by now, appellant has
completed more than 5 years 6 months of incarceration without
remission. 
6. Considering the above, we are of the view that the sentence
may be suspended and the appellant may be enlarged on bail.
7. Accordingly, sentence of the appellant as modified by the High
2

## Page 465

Court stands suspended.
8. Consequently, We direct that the appellant shall be produced
before the learned VIII Additional Sessions Judge, Sagar within a
maximum period of 7 days from today who shall thereafter enlarge
the appellant on bail on such terms and conditions as may be deemed
appropriate.
9. List the appeal for hearing in due course.

pending  before  the  Court  of  Additional  Principal

Haryana  to  the  Court  of  Principal  Judge,  Family
Court, Nohar, Dist. Hanumangarh, Rajasthan."

perusal of the material on record, we find that the petitioner has

Hanumangarh, Rajasthan.

PETITION(S) FOR SPECIAL LEAVE TO APPEAL (C)  NO(S).  25714/2026

## Page 521

2
2. The facts of the case reveal that the petitioner was selected
to  join  the  Indian  Air  Force  as  an  Agniveer  Vayu  (science
subjects). However, on account of a medical disability, she was not
permitted to join the Indian Air Force. The petitioner preferred an
appeal before the Appellate Medical Board, which also held her
unfit to join the Indian Air Force. Thereafter, the petitioner
obtained opinions from the All India Institute of Medical Sciences,
New Delhi, as well as another Government institute, and was found
fit to join the Indian Air Force. The High Court dismissed her Writ
Petition (Civil) No.2031/2026, relying upon the medical opinions of
the Medical Board as well as the Appellate Medical Board.
3. This Court, in order to ascertain whether the petitioner was
medically fit to join the Indian Air Force as an Agniveer Vayu, has
requested the Director of the All India Institute of Medical
Sciences to examine the petitioner. A report has since been
received  vide letter dated 13.08.2026, which does not hold the
petitioner medically unfit to join the Indian Air Force as an
Agniveer Vayu (science subjects).
4. Mrs.  Archana  Pathak  Dave,  learned  Additional  Solicitor
General, has informed this Court that the course has already
commenced on 01.07.2026 and that it would be practically impossible
to permit the petitioner to join the ongoing course along with her
batchmates, who have already joined. However, Mrs. Archana Pathak
Dave, learned Additional Solicitor General, was fair enough to
state before this Court that the petitioner would be permitted to
PETITION(S) FOR SPECIAL LEAVE TO APPEAL (C)  NO(S).  25714/2026

## Page 522

3
join the next course, which is likely to commence in December 2026
or January 2027.
5. In light of the statement made by the learned ASG, the
respondents are directed to permit the petitioner to join the next
course, which is likely to commence in December 2026 or January
2027.
6. The learned ASG has also prayed that, in future, whenever a
Special Medical Board is constituted under the orders of this
Court, a specialist from the Research and Referral Hospital or a
senior officer from the Office of the Directorate General Armed
Forces Medical Services (DGAFMS), should be made a part of such
Special Medical Board, thereby enabling the civilian authorities to
take into consideration the Army, Navy and Air Force manuals, which
provide for the detailed procedure for medical examination. The
prayer made is a genuine prayer and the Union of India shall be
free to make such a request in future as and when such contingency
arises in cases requiring medical examination.
7. The respondents are directed to pass necessary consequential
orders within a period of 45 days from today.
8.  With the aforesaid, the petition stands disposed of.
9.  Pending application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

2
admitted before us that indeed he is in arrears. However,
according to him, he has gone bankrupt and is not in a
position to pay a single penny for maintenance of his wife and
daughter.
4. We have made ourselves very abundantly clear today before
the Respondent that he has to arrange at least for 50% of the
arrears amount i.e. Rs.14,00,000/- (Rupees Fourteen Lakh) to
be paid to the petitioner within a period of four weeks from
today. In the event if this amount is not paid, we shall
proceed on the next date to pass an order dissolving the
marriage between the parties in exercise of our jurisdiction
under Article 142 of the Constitution.
5. Insofar as the visitation rights of the Respondent are
concerned, Pahul has been gracious enough to convey to us that
as and when she gets time, she would definitely have a meeting
with her father. She would make all possible endeavors to see
that at least once in a week she talks with her father.
6. If the Respondent pays this amount to the petitioner
within four weeks, we shall again take up this matter for
further hearing and continue with this arrangement as provided
earlier by our order dated 19-5-2025.
7. We once again make it clear that in the event of failure,
we shall dissolve the marriage and put an end to all the
proceedings  between  the  parties.  The  only  arrangement
thereafter that we shall provide for would be visitation
rights so far as Pahul is concerned and maintenance.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Pursuant to the order dated 30.07.2026 passed by this Court, the
contemnor has filed an affidavit under which she has tendered unconditional
apology and to demonstrate her bona fides, she has stated in her affidavit that
she would abide by the settlement agreement entered into between the parties
and she would unequivocally and unconditionally withdraw FIR No.561/2025
dated 18.04.2025 registered at Police Station : Sarkanda, District : Bilaspur,
Chhattisgarh and she has further deposed that she will take all steps as may be
necessary in law for withdrawal of the said FIR and all proceedings arising
1

## Page 626

therefrom and connected thereto. She has also prayed for protection from this
Court being extended to her by contending that parties bound by the
settlement agreement should not pursue or initiate any civil or criminal
proceedings whatsoever viz., arising out of Memorandum of understanding /
Settlement Agreement dated 31.12.2024 and recorded thereunder; and the
petitioner should withdraw the legal notice dated 26.05.2025 sent to her and
her mother on behalf of the company whereunder they have intimated the
contemnor that they would initiate civil and criminal action against them. 
2. At this stage, it would suffice to state that this litigation seems to be an
ongoing and continuous litigation without there being an end as could be seen
from the conduct of the parties. Be that as it may, it would be suffice to state
that in view of the categorical undertaking given that the FIR filed by the
contemnor would be withdrawn, any further litigation arising out of the said FIR
either at the instance of the contemnor herself or at the instance of the
complainant(s) would not be warranted and we make it clear that neither the
complainant(s) nor their predecessors nor their assignees would proceed further
against the contemnor as indicated in the legal notice dated 26.05.2025.
However, we make it clear that the complainant(s) would be at liberty to seek
for enforcement of the Memorandum of Understanding / Settlement Agreement
dated 31.12.2024 and the settlement recorded thereunder in accordance with
law and we make no further order in that regard in these proceedings. The
closure of the contempt proceedings will arise only after FIR No.561/2025 dated
18.04.2025 being withdrawn. Hence, list this matter after four weeks for passing
further orders including award of cost of the present contempt proceedings.

2. It is not in dispute that the mother of the appellant
has passed away.
3. In such view of the matter, the aforesaid condition
stands temporarily relaxed and the appellant is permitted
to visit his village between 21.08.2026 and 27.08.2026.
4. Accordingly,  the  Interlocutory  Application  stands
disposed of.

## Page 1010

3. It is the contention of the learned counsel appearing for the
petitioner that petitioner has been disqualified  for not conducting four meetings
of the  Gram Sabha for the financial year 01.04.2024 to 01.04.2025  and the
impugned order/judgment has been passed on the basis of a notice which was
issued under Section 14(1)(j-3) of the Maharashtra Village Panchayats Act, 1959
(“for short Act”). We notice from the impugned order/judgment at page 08
paragraph 09 a finding has been returned that petitioner was served with the
notice for disqualification proceedings under Section 7 of the Act. At this
juncture, the learned counsel appearing for the respondent no.4(complainant)
had drawn our attention to the reply submitted by the petitioner to the show
cause notice to contend that petitioner has traversed in his reply to the notice
with regard to non-conducting of four meetings in a financial year, which would
imply that the notice for disqualification was in fact, issued to the petitioner.
Hence, to ascertain as to whether, a notice seeking to disqualify the petitioner
for not conducting the four meetings in a financial year as contemplated under
Section 7 of the Act, we are issuing notice to respondent Nos. 1 to 3for the said
limited purpose. It is also made clear that in the event of notice under Section 7
of the Act had been issued, there ends the matter and no further scrutiny of the
impugned order/judgment would be warranted as otherwise it may require
examination.
4. For the aforesaid limited purpose, we issue notice to the respondent
Nos. 1 to 3, returnable in four weeks.
